prompt: Why is a confined process called a thin wall?

choices.text: It shares the kernel with the rest of the machine
choices.why: Right: one kernel flaw crosses every such wall.

choices.text: Because it lets the program use the network
choices.why: A confined process can be denied the network entirely.

choices.text: Because it can only be built by root on a running system
choices.why: Who builds it says nothing about its strength.

choices.text: Because it disappears when the program ends
choices.why: A virtual machine snapshot disappears too, and is a thick wall.

prompt: Order these layers from the thinnest wall to the thickest.
A file may have been built to escape whatever holds it. Where should it be opened?

choices.text: In a systemd-run sandbox on the firm's portal server
choices.why: That wall shares the server's kernel, the very thing it might attack.

choices.text: In a container next to the production containers
choices.why: Same kernel as production.

choices.text: In a virtual machine or on a machine set aside
choices.why: Right: a thick wall for what may be built to escape.

choices.text: On the analyst's own workstation, which has antivirus
choices.why: An antivirus is not a wall.

prompt: Why does the lesson write its own suspicious file instead of using a real malicious one?

choices.text: No lesson needs a dangerous one
choices.why: Right: a harmless file that tries the same things shows the walls.

choices.text: Because real malware does not run on Ubuntu
choices.why: Plenty does.

choices.text: Because sandboxes only stop scripts written in bash
choices.why: They stop whatever runs inside them.

choices.text: Because the lab has no internet to download one
choices.why: Even with internet the lesson would not use one.

prompt: You wrote relatorio.sh and know it is harmless. Why does the lesson still say not to run it outside a sandbox?

choices.text: Because it would delete the SSH keys
choices.why: It only lists names.

choices.text: Because bash refuses scripts that write to /etc
choices.why: Root's bash writes to /etc happily.

choices.text: For the day you turn out to be wrong about a file
choices.why: Right: the one time it matters is when you were sure.

choices.text: Because the lab forbids running scripts as ana
choices.why: ana runs scripts all through the course.

prompt: Match each attempt of relatorio.sh to the option that stopped it.
With ProtectHome=tmpfs, how can the program still read relatorio.sh from ana's home?

choices.text: ProtectHome only hides directories, never files
choices.why: It replaces the whole home with an empty one.

choices.text: Because --uid=ana makes ProtectHome skip ana's own home
choices.why: ProtectHome hides every home, the runner's included.

choices.text: bash reads scripts before the sandbox is built
choices.why: The sandbox exists before bash starts.

choices.text: BindReadOnlyPaths puts that one file back, read-only
choices.why: Right: read-only, and nothing else.

prompt: Inside the sandbox the script still printed done. What does that show?

choices.text: Walls limit what it touches, not whether it runs
choices.why: Right: it needs no idea what the program is.

choices.text: That the sandbox failed to stop it
choices.why: All three attempts failed; the walls held.

choices.text: That the script detected the sandbox and gave up
choices.why: It simply carried on after each failure.

choices.text: That NoNewPrivileges let the last line of the script through
choices.why: Printing a word needs no privilege.

prompt: Why trace a suspicious program inside the sandbox rather than just running it there?

choices.text: Because strace makes the walls thicker
choices.why: It only watches.

choices.text: Because the sandbox does not work without it
choices.why: The sandbox held without strace in the last section.

choices.text: The trace records what the walls hid
choices.why: Right: the files and addresses it reached for are the findings.

choices.text: To slow it down so it cannot finish
choices.why: Slowing it is a side effect, not the point.

prompt: Match each answer the kernel gave in the trace to its cause.

pairs.right: the file is not in this world
there is no route, because there is no network

prompt: The tool that prints every system call a program makes, with the kernel's answer, is ___.
What does firejail's --whitelist=~/relatorio.sh do to the home directory?

choices.text: Deletes everything in it except that file
choices.why: Nothing is deleted; it is a view.

choices.text: Makes the file executable for every user
choices.why: Permissions are not touched.

choices.text: Copies the file to a disposable machine
choices.why: It stays on web, confined.

choices.text: Shows only the named path inside the sandbox
choices.why: Right: the program sees what it was given.

prompt: What does a disposable machine give that a confined process does not?

choices.text: Whatever the file did is thrown away with the machine
choices.why: Right: and the file never had the production machine to work on.

choices.text: A faster way to open large files
choices.why: Speed is not the point.

choices.text: Protection from flaws in the hypervisor
choices.why: A virtual machine still depends on the hypervisor.

choices.text: An automatic verdict on whether the file is malicious
choices.why: That is what lesson 19's services try to give.

prompt: What does systemd-analyze security measure?

choices.text: How much sandboxing the unit uses
choices.why: Right: from 0, confined, to 10, not at all.

choices.text: How many vulnerabilities the service's program has
choices.why: It knows nothing about bugs; that is lesson 16.

choices.text: How long the service takes to start
choices.why: That is systemd-analyze blame.

choices.text: Whether the service's port is open from outside
choices.why: Ports are lesson 1's scan.

prompt: After adding the sandbox drop-in, what does the lesson check before the new score?

choices.text: That the drop-in file is owned by root
choices.why: It was copied with sudo; ownership is not the risk.

choices.text: That systemd printed no warning on reload
choices.why: A silent reload says nothing about the portal working.

choices.text: That the portal still answers
choices.why: Right: a sandbox that breaks the job is removed in a hurry.

choices.text: That the score is below 5
choices.why: The score comes last, and is a guide.

prompt: A colleague wants every unit on the server scored 0 before the next audit. What is wrong with that goal?

choices.text: Nothing: 0 is the safest possible service
choices.why: Some checks do not apply, and some walls break the job.

choices.text: The score is a guide, not a target
choices.why: Right: take away what the job does not need, not what the score asks.

choices.text: A score of 0 is impossible on Ubuntu
choices.why: That is not the objection.

choices.text: Auditors only accept scores between 4 and 6
choices.why: No auditor rule says so.

prompt: How many separate attempts did relatorio.sh make that the sandbox refused?
Which of these lines in 20-sandbox.conf would break the portal if it were later changed to call an API on another machine? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: ProtectHome=yes
choices.why: The portal's home is /srv/portal, and an API call needs no home.

choices.text: RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_INET AF_UNIX
choices.why: An IPv4 call is AF_INET, which is allowed.

choices.text: NoNewPrivileges=yes
choices.why: Calling an API needs no new privilege.

choices.text: The IPAddressDeny=any from lesson 10, if both drop-ins are installed
choices.why: That one denies every address but localhost.

prompt: A client mails an unknown spreadsheet with macros, and the accountant must see its contents today. What is the best first step from this lesson?

choices.text: Open it on the accountant's own workstation with macros off
choices.why: That puts an unknown file on a machine full of client data.

choices.text: Run it with systemd-run on the portal server
choices.why: The portal server is the last place for an unknown file.

choices.text: Forward it to everybody so that more people can judge it
choices.why: That spreads the risk, not the judgement.

choices.text: Open it on a disposable machine set aside for it
choices.why: Right: whatever it does goes away with the machine.

prompt: What does PrivateTmp=yes protect against?

choices.text: The program filling the disk with temporary files
choices.why: Its /tmp still uses disk; it is only private.

choices.text: Other machines on the segment reading the program's files
choices.why: /tmp is never shared across machines.

choices.text: Sharing /tmp with other programs
choices.why: Right: nothing it leaves there, or finds there, crosses the wall.

choices.text: The program running as root
choices.why: That is the account, not /tmp.

prompt: ProtectSystem=___ makes the whole file system read-only for the service.
What exposure score did systemd-analyze give the portal before the drop-in?
